summary: We built Little Astro’s Adventure, a browser-based 3D Moon-base game for kids 7–12. Players balance life support, power and communication delay, where saving battery risks crew health or missed Earth messages. No choice is free, so trade-offs become tangible. It builds understanding of real deep-space survival decisions through hands-on play.
details:
1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

Little Astro's Adventure is a browser-based 3D Moon-base survival game for kids 7–12. The player registers as a Commander, picks a mission category, lands on the Moon and visits department buildings. Category A covers life support, power budgeting and communication delay, and Category B is planned to add food production and radiation shielding. All units share one battery. The player can run Life Support and Communication at full power or put one in battery-saving mode. Saving mode drains the battery slower, but CO₂ rises, oxygen and temperature fall, crew members can fall ill, and Earth's replies become slow and noisy. Random events like leaks, dust storms, power surges and moonquakes force quick decisions. The player wins by keeping the crew alive until the rescue ship arrives.

2. What benefits does it offer?

Kids learn by doing, and they can fail safely: they can retry, ask Mission Control for tips, and see a short "Remember" lesson after each event. Text is in plain language and the game runs in any browser with no download.

3. What is the intended impact?

Kids leave understanding that survival in space means trade-offs, because every resource choice has a cost. We want to spark interest in space and engineering, for use at home or in the classroom.

4. What tools did you use?

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js for the 3D scenes (Moon surface, base, astronauts) and GSAP for camera movement. Textures are generated in code and sounds are made with the Web Audio API. Accounts and progress are stored in the browser with localStorage. We worked in VS Code with Git and a local server for testing. If your team used an AI assistant (Claude) for coding help, I'd mention it here, since hackathons usually expect AI use to be disclosed.

5. How is your project creative?

Instead of a quiz or a dashboard, kids walk around a 3D lunar base and step inside its buildings. No choice is free: saving power can make an astronaut ill, and Earth's supply messages are missed if the radio is in saving mode. Events come from a shuffled set, so each run plays differently. An astronaut avatar tells the story and guides the player, and the pages share a cinematic space look.

6. What factors did your team consider?

We considered the 7–12 age range (short text, plain words, terms explained in context) and kept the number of core systems small so nothing feels overwhelming. We also designed failure to feel useful (hints, retries, lessons) and made sure every option has a cost. For accessibility, we added a sound on/off option, reduced-motion support in the intro pages, and layouts for phone and desktop.
